title: The Yes Machine
author: Is It Working?!
summary: Responding to Adam Grant's public reframing of his own people-pleasing as self-focused rather than kind, this piece agrees with Grant's individual diagnosis but argues it only tells half the story at work, where the incentives making 'yes' the rational choice are real and measurable, not just psychological habit. It marshals a wall of research to make this case: agreeableness carries a documented earnings penalty (disagreeable men out-earn agreeable men by about 18%, roughly $9,772 a year), women disproportionately end up holding low-promotability 'office housework' tasks partly because they're asked more and accept more often, and 85% of employees report situations where they felt unable to raise an important issue with a supervisor. Its most striking finding comes from Vanessa Bohns's research: across studies with more than 14,000 strangers, people asking for things underestimate how often others will comply by an average of 48%, meaning every manager in an organization is systematically unaware of how much coercive weight their requests actually carry. The piece's sharpest move is to reject 'learn to say no' as advice, calling it a way of putting the entire remedial burden on the person with the least power in the exchange, and instead proposes structural fixes — auditing who gets asked to do low-promotability work, making 'citizenship' contributions count visibly rather than silently informing ratings, training requesters to recognize their own outsized influence, and watching what actually happens to people after they decline something.

Shows 85% of employees report situations where they felt unable to raise an important issue with a supervisor — mostly from fear of being labeled negatively, not apathy.
Rejects 'learn to say no' as advice, calling it a way to put the entire remedial burden on the least powerful person in the exchange rather than fixing who gets asked what.
quotes: Chronic people pleasing, he argues, isn't rooted in concern for other people but in a need for their approval... 'It's not about their feelings; it's about how their feelings make us feel.'
Disagreeable men out-earned agreeable men by around 18%, roughly US$9,772 a year; for women the gap was closer to 5%, or US$1,828. It turns out that being nice can be priced, annually, in cash.
85% reported situations where they felt unable to raise an issue with a supervisor despite believing it mattered. Only 51% said they generally felt comfortable speaking up at all.
Across studies involving more than 14,000 strangers, requesters underestimated compliance by an average of 48%. People say yes vastly more often than askers predict.

An organisation that requires acts of personal courage to surface routine information has built a culture and a machine that runs on the cost of saying no - and then sends its people on a course to fix themselves.
